I feel like when I'm doing campaign events, I get boring and I lose people because I like to talk about the structure of the Constitution. But that really is what should be guiding all of these conversations. And I get nerdy about this. are governments designed so that the government has to protect the freedoms of the people. And when the government gets out of whack, then they can start violating people's freedom. But not only do we have a federalist system where most of the power belongs to the states and only enumerated powers belong to the federal government, but within the federal government, that power is divided between branches. Sorry, between branches. And those branches are supposed to jealously check each other to make sure that no branch gets too powerful because if one of the branches is more powerful than the others, then that branch can violate people's liberties. And right now the executive branch is too powerful. And Congress has been complicit in creating this problem. And then Congress has also been derelict in not fixing this problem. So all of the agencies are created by Congress. Congress gives them a statutory authority. They pass a law that says we're creating this agency and this is what it's supposed to do. And there are good arguments for some of these agencies existing. But what happens after they're created is that they want to grow. Bureaucracy always wants to grow, and the agencies want bigger budgets, they want to be more relevant, they want more of a mission, and they just keep creeping outside that statutory authority. And what I think the solution is, I think it's time for Congress to go look at every agency's statutory authority, compare that to what they're doing, and go in line by line in their budget and defund everything every agency's doing that's outside that statutory authority. It would also go a long way towards solving our government overreach problems. And almost all the problems people want me to talk to them about or want Congress to solve are really government overreach problems at their root. So talking about statutory authority and how agencies got created isn't as exciting as going in and promising to abolish agencies. But in my adult lifetime, I've watched a lot of candidates for president and for Congress. Give a list of agencies, they're going to abolish, and I've never seen anyone actually abolish one. And so then we just end up in the same place. I think we can make real progress by just holding the agencies accountable and putting them back in their statutory boxes.
